questions.stem: Under the United Nations World Tourism Organization definition used in VCE Geography, a tourist travels outside their usual environment for:
options: more than 24 hours but not more than one consecutive year
at least one week but no longer than six consecutive months
any length of time, as long as they cross a national border
more than 12 hours, so long as the trip is for leisure only
questions.explanation: The definition sets a lower limit of 24 hours and an upper limit of one consecutive year away from the usual environment. Travel within one's own country counts, so crossing a border is not required.

questions.stem: Using the UNWTO definition, which of these people is a tourist?
options: a Geelong resident commuting to work in Melbourne daily
a day-tripper who visits the Dandenongs and returns that night
a student who moves to London to study for three years
a Melburnian spending three nights at Lakes Entrance
questions.explanation: Three nights away is more than 24 hours and less than a year, so it counts. The day-tripper stays less than 24 hours, the commuter is within their usual environment, and three years exceeds the one-year limit.

questions.stem: A Perth family taking a holiday in Broome is an example of:
options: inbound tourism
outbound tourism
international tourism
domestic tourism
questions.explanation: Domestic tourism is travel within one's own country. Inbound and outbound tourism both involve crossing an international border.

questions.stem: From Australia's point of view, a family from Singapore visiting the Great Barrier Reef is part of:
options: domestic tourism within Australia
excursionist day-trip travel
inbound international tourism
outbound international tourism
questions.explanation: Inbound tourism is visitors arriving from overseas; outbound tourism is Australians travelling abroad. For Singapore, the same trip would count as outbound tourism.

questions.stem: Compared with domestic tourism, international tourism typically involves:
options: passports, visas, currency exchange and usually longer travel distances
travel that always lasts less than 24 hours from leaving home to returning
no need for transport infrastructure such as airports or seaports
visitors who share the same national laws as the host community
questions.explanation: Crossing borders brings visa rules, currency exchange and often greater absolute and cultural distance. Domestic tourists travel within their own country and so remain under the same national laws.

questions.stem: Ecotourism is best described as:
options: large-scale package tourism to resorts that were built on cleared natural land
tourism to places associated with death, disaster or human suffering
nature-based tourism that conserves environments, educates visitors and benefits local people
any tourism that takes place outdoors, such as beach holidays, theme park stays and ski holidays in the Alps
questions.explanation: Ecotourism combines nature-based experiences with conservation, interpretation and local benefit. Simply being outdoors does not make tourism ecotourism, and tourism to sites of suffering is dark tourism.

questions.stem: Visiting the Auschwitz-Birkenau Memorial and Museum in Poland is an example of:
options: adventure tourism
wellness tourism
dark tourism
ecotourism
questions.explanation: Dark tourism involves travel to places associated with death, tragedy or atrocity, often for remembrance and education. Such sites need respectful management of visitor behaviour.

questions.stem: Queenstown in New Zealand is known for bungy jumping, jet boating and skiing. This makes it a centre of:
options: heritage tourism
adventure tourism
dark tourism
medical tourism
questions.explanation: Adventure tourism involves physical challenge and some perceived risk in a natural setting. Queenstown's landforms, lakes and rivers support these activities.

questions.stem: Budj Bim in south-west Victoria, World Heritage listed for the Gunditjmara people's ancient system of eel traps and channels, mainly attracts:
options: event and sports tourism
cruise ship tourism
cultural and heritage tourism
snow and alpine tourism
questions.explanation: Visitors come to learn about the Gunditjmara people's aquaculture system and continuing culture, often on tours led by Gunditjmara guides. This is cultural and heritage tourism.

questions.stem: Which world region has long received the largest share of international tourist arrivals?
options: Oceania
Europe
Africa
South America
questions.explanation: Europe has many countries close together, high incomes, dense transport links and many cultural attractions, so short international trips are common. Asia and the Pacific has grown fastest in recent decades.

questions.stem: Victoria's snow tourism is concentrated at alpine resorts such as Falls Creek and Mount Hotham mainly because:
options: their high elevation gives cold winters with regular snowfall
they are the closest resorts of any kind to central Melbourne
they receive the highest summer temperatures in the state
they lie on the coast, where winter storms bring heavy snow
questions.explanation: Snow tourism depends on a natural characteristic, elevation, which makes winters cold enough for snow. Distance from Melbourne is several hours' drive, so proximity is not the reason.

questions.stem: Ethical tourism is tourism that:
options: respects host cultures, treats workers and animals fairly and benefits locals
takes place only in national parks, marine parks and other protected natural areas of a country
is organised by large international companies to keep prices low
avoids any contact between visitors and members of the host community
questions.explanation: Ethical tourism focuses on the rights and welfare of host communities, workers and animals, and on fair sharing of benefits. It can occur in cities or natural areas, and it usually seeks respectful contact rather than none.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes ethical tourism from ecotourism?
options: ethical tourism centres on the welfare of people, cultures and animals; ecotourism on natural areas
ethical tourism must take place in natural areas; ecotourism must take place in cities
ethical tourism is always domestic; ecotourism is always international
ethical tourism aims to maximise visitor numbers; ecotourism aims to minimise the benefits to local people
questions.explanation: The two overlap, but ecotourism is defined by nature-based experience and conservation, while ethical tourism is defined by fair and respectful treatment of people, cultures and animals in any setting. Neither is limited to domestic or international travel.

questions.stem: A volunteer program lets tourists spend a week caring for children at an orphanage overseas. Child welfare organisations criticise such programs mainly because they:
options: are always run by the national government of the host country
are too expensive for most young Australian travellers to join
can encourage children to be separated from families to attract paying visitors
give the children too few chances to meet and learn from people from other countries
questions.explanation: Demand from paying volunteers can create an incentive to keep or recruit children in institutions, and short-term carers can harm children's attachment. This is a key issue in ethical tourism.

questions.stem: A traveller wanting to see elephants in Thailand ethically would be best advised to choose:
options: a street performance where elephants are walked through traffic
a circus where elephants are trained to perform tricks daily
a sanctuary where visitors watch elephants without riding them
a camp offering elephant rides and elephant painting shows
questions.explanation: Ethical tourism considers animal welfare, and riding and performances usually involve harsh training and confinement. Observation-based sanctuaries aim to let animals behave more naturally.

questions.stem: Which describes a long-term change in international tourism since the 1950s?
options: a large growth in arrivals and a widening range of destinations
a steady fall in arrivals as the cost of air travel kept rising
a shift of most arrivals away from Europe to Antarctica
a narrowing of tourism to wealthy travellers on ocean liners
questions.explanation: International arrivals have grown many times over since the 1950s, and destinations have spread from Europe and North America to Asia, the Pacific and beyond. Air travel became cheaper, not dearer, over this period.

questions.stem: Wide-bodied jet aircraft such as the Boeing 747, in service from 1970, changed tourism mainly by:
options: making ocean liners the cheapest way to travel between continents
cutting the cost and time of long-haul flights, opening distant places to mass tourism
replacing all domestic road travel within Australia with short, cheap air journeys between cities
ending the need for any airports in regional tourist destinations
questions.explanation: Larger, more efficient aircraft lowered the cost per seat and shortened journeys, reducing the relative distance between places such as Australia and Europe. This helped long-haul travel become mass tourism.

questions.stem: The growth of low-cost airlines such as Jetstar and AirAsia has mainly:
options: made short international trips affordable for many more people, especially in Asia
reduced the total number of tourists travelling within Australia and across South-East Asia
limited air travel to business travellers able to pay full fares
replaced the need for tourist accommodation in destinations
questions.explanation: By cutting fares, low-cost carriers opened air travel to people on lower and middle incomes and boosted short trips within Asia. They increased rather than reduced travel in the region.

questions.stem: A coastal village was first visited by a few backpackers. Later, locals opened guesthouses. Then foreign firms built large resorts and visitor numbers rose rapidly. In Butler's Tourism Area Life Cycle, the village is now in the:
options: exploration stage
involvement stage
decline stage
development stage
questions.explanation: Exploration is the backpacker phase and involvement is when locals begin providing services. Rapid growth with outside investment and large facilities marks the development stage.

questions.stem: In Butler's Tourism Area Life Cycle, a resort with flat visitor numbers, ageing hotels and declining environmental quality is most likely in the:
options: exploration stage
involvement stage
development stage
stagnation stage
questions.explanation: Stagnation occurs when a destination reaches or exceeds its capacity and growth stops. Without rejuvenation, such as new attractions, it may move into decline.

questions.stem: For a Melbourne family, which is a push factor encouraging a winter holiday in Queensland?
options: the coral reefs off Cairns and Port Douglas
Melbourne's cold, wet winter weather
Queensland's warm, sunny winter climate
the theme parks on the Gold Coast
questions.explanation: Push factors are conditions at the place of origin that encourage people to leave. Queensland's warmth, theme parks and reefs are pull factors that attract visitors to the destination.

questions.stem: Which is a human characteristic of Hobart that attracts tourists?
options: the city's mild summer climate
the Museum of Old and New Art (MONA)
the view from the summit of kunanyi/Mount Wellington
the deep, sheltered estuary of the Derwent River
questions.explanation: Human characteristics are made or shaped by people, such as galleries, events and heritage buildings. Mountains, rivers and climate are natural characteristics of a host destination.

questions.stem: Online booking platforms and social media have changed tourism mainly by:
options: making it impossible for small towns to attract visitors from overseas
requiring tourists to travel only in large organised groups
letting travellers plan and book independently and spreading images of places
ending all demand for travel agents and tour companies around the world almost overnight
questions.explanation: Communication technology lets people compare and book flights and accommodation themselves, and shared images can make little-known places popular quickly. Travel agents still operate, though their role has changed.

questions.stem: The Schengen Agreement affects tourism in Europe by:
options: setting a single price for hotel rooms across every country of Europe
banning tourists from outside Europe from visiting member countries
requiring all visitors to travel between countries only by rail
allowing travel between most member countries without border passport checks
questions.explanation: Schengen is an international agreement that removed routine border controls between participating countries, making multi-country trips easier. Visitors from outside still enter, subject to visa rules.

questions.stem: Australia's working holiday visa program encourages youth tourism mainly because it:
options: requires young visitors to stay only in the capital cities
lets young visitors from partner countries work to fund longer stays
gives young Australians free flights to partner countries in Europe
limits young visitors to trips of less than one week in length
questions.explanation: This national policy, built on reciprocal agreements with partner countries, lets young travellers combine work and travel, so they stay longer and spread spending across regions. Australians can use reciprocal visas overseas.

questions.stem: Bhutan charges international visitors a daily Sustainable Development Fee as part of a 'high value, low volume' tourism policy. The main purpose of this policy is to:
options: prevent any international visitors from entering the country at all
limit visitor numbers while funding conservation and community benefits
attract the largest possible number of visitors to earn foreign currency
ensure that all tourism profits go to foreign-owned hotel chains
questions.explanation: The fee discourages mass tourism and directs revenue to services such as conservation, health and education. It reflects a national policy choice to put sustainability ahead of visitor numbers.

questions.stem: The rise of 'grey nomads' touring Australia by caravan reflects which factor affecting tourism?
options: a major event held in one city that attracts visitors for a single week
foreign investment in large resorts in Australia's capital cities
changing lifestyles, with more healthy, active retirees with time to travel
international agreements that remove passport checks between states
questions.explanation: An ageing population with savings, superannuation and good health has more time for long domestic trips. This is a change in income and lifestyle rather than a policy or event.

questions.stem: The rapid growth of outbound tourism from China since the 1990s is best explained by:
options: a large fall in China's population that freed time for travel
the closure of all tourist attractions within mainland China
the removal of all visa requirements for Chinese citizens worldwide
rising middle-class incomes and an easing of limits on overseas travel
questions.explanation: Higher incomes and agreements allowing group and later independent travel to approved destinations made China a major source of international tourists. Visa requirements still apply for many destinations.

questions.stem: Large integrated resorts with casinos, hotels and convention centres opened in Singapore in 2010 and drew many more visitors. This mainly shows the effect on tourism of:
options: a change in the climate
investment and marketing
a natural disaster
an international border agreement
questions.explanation: Large-scale investment created new human attractions, supported by marketing to international visitors. These facilities changed the destination's tourism characteristics without any change in its natural environment.

questions.stem: Melbourne hosting the Australian Open tennis each January is an example of:
options: event tourism
dark tourism
ecotourism
medical tourism
questions.explanation: Event tourism is travel to attend a major sporting, cultural or business event. It brings a peak of visitors at a set time each year.

questions.stem: After the 2002 Bali bombings, visitor arrivals to Bali fell sharply for a time and later recovered. This shows that:
options: tourism in Bali depends only on its natural characteristics
domestic tourism always falls faster than international tourism
security events can cause short-term falls in tourism at a destination
terrorism permanently ends international tourism to an affected place
questions.explanation: Regional occurrences such as political and security events change perceptions of safety and can reduce arrivals for a period. Bali's recovery shows the effect was not permanent.

questions.stem: In summer 2019–20, many tourism businesses on the New South Wales south coast and in East Gippsland lost visitors even where they had not been burnt. The best explanation is that:
options: the fires made the region's beaches permanently unsafe for swimming
the region's tourism depends mainly on winter snow sports
international border closures had already stopped all travel
fire, smoke and road closures deterred visitors from the wider region
questions.explanation: A regional disaster affects perceptions and access across a whole area, not just the burnt sites. The losses over that summer came before the COVID-19 border closures of March 2020.

questions.stem: When Australia's international border closed in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic, many Australians who would have holidayed overseas travelled at home instead. Once intrastate travel was allowed, the likely effect on regional tourism was:
options: a fall in domestic visitors as overseas travel replaced it
more domestic visitors, partly offsetting the loss of international visitors
a rise in inbound international visitors to regional Australia from nearby countries
a permanent end to tourism in all regional parts of Australia
questions.explanation: With outbound travel blocked, some spending shifted to domestic trips, helping many regional destinations. Inbound international visitors could not arrive while the border was closed.

questions.stem: Many Australians feel the United Kingdom is 'close' because of a shared language and customs, although it is on the other side of the world. This is an example of:
options: cultural distance
absolute distance
relative location
spatial association
questions.explanation: Cultural distance is the degree of similarity in attitudes and social norms, so places far apart in kilometres can feel close. Absolute distance is measured in units such as kilometres.

questions.stem: A new freeway cuts the driving time from Melbourne to a coastal town from three hours to two. In terms of distance, this has reduced the town's:
options: absolute distance from Melbourne
cultural distance from Melbourne
latitude and longitude
relative distance from Melbourne
questions.explanation: Relative distance considers time, cost or convenience, so a faster road brings the town 'closer' even though the kilometres are similar. This can increase weekend visits from the city.

questions.stem: A map shows Victoria's alpine resorts at high elevations reached by sealed alpine roads, with no resorts on high peaks that lack road access. This pattern best illustrates:
options: a strong spatial association between snow tourism and coastal location
that snow tourism depends on road access alone, regardless of elevation
that elevation has no relationship with where snow tourism has developed
a spatial association between snow tourism and both elevation and road access
questions.explanation: Resorts occur where a natural factor (elevation) and a human factor (road access) coincide, showing the interconnection of factors. Neither factor alone explains the distribution.

questions.stem: A hotel booking app showing nearby rooms on a map using the phone's location relies mainly on:
options: choropleth maps and census data
contour lines and cross-sections
aerial photographs and transects
GNSS positioning and digital mapping
questions.explanation: The phone uses a Global Navigation Satellite System such as GPS to find its location, and a mapping platform displays nearby places. This is a common use of geospatial technology by the tourism industry.

questions.stem: A national park uses anonymised mobile phone location data to map where visitors gather throughout the day. This mainly helps managers to:
options: learn each visitor's name and home address for marketing
measure the depth of the park's lakes and rivers
predict the weather conditions in the park each day
identify crowded sites and times to plan facilities and staff
questions.explanation: Mapping visitor density shows where and when pressure is greatest, guiding decisions on parking, toilets, rangers and track upgrades. The data is anonymised, so it does not identify individuals.

questions.stem: A geographer uses geotagged social media photos to map where tourists go in a city. A key limitation of this data is that:
options: geotags give no information at all about a photo's location
the photos can be mapped only at a global scale, never a local one
the data counts every visitor, including those who never post
only visitors who post photos are counted, so the sample is biased
questions.explanation: Assessing data reliability matters: people who post photos differ from those who do not, and popular photo spots are over-represented. The data shows patterns of posting, not of all visitors.

questions.stem: A walking track runs from a visitor centre to a lookout that lies midway between south and south-west of it. The direction of the lookout from the visitor centre is:
options: WSW
SW
SSW
SSE
questions.explanation: On the sixteen-point compass, the point midway between S and SW is south-south-west (SSW). WSW lies between W and SW, on the other side of SW.

questions.stem: Visitor numbers at a regional festival rose from 40 000 one year to 50 000 the next. The percentage increase was:
questions.explanation: Percentage change = (50 000 − 40 000)/40 000 × 100 = 25%. Dividing the increase by the new total gives 20%, a common error.

questions.stem: In a survey of 200 visitors at Wilsons Promontory, 70 came from Melbourne, 50 from regional Victoria, 50 from interstate and 30 from overseas. What percentage were international visitors?
questions.explanation: International visitors are those from overseas: 30/200 × 100 = 15%. Adding the interstate visitors gives 40%, but interstate visitors are domestic tourists.

questions.stem: A student surveys visitors at a beach resort only on one weekday morning in winter. The main weakness of this survey design is that it:
options: will count too many summer visitors, making totals unrealistically high
cannot be analysed because the survey has a fixed location
will give exactly the same results as a summer weekend survey
will under-represent peak-season visitors, so results are less reliable
questions.explanation: Survey design must consider the times, durations and locations of sampling, since visitor types change across seasons and days of the week. A single winter weekday misses the summer and weekend crowds.
